note: Subjects/Maths/M1 Mechanics 1/4 Dynamics of a particle moving in a straight line or plane.md
outline: A force changes motion according to Newton’s laws. Draw separate force diagrams and apply $\sum\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$, resolving along chosen axes. Connected particles share the magnitude of acceleration while a light string over a smooth pulley has one tension. On an incline, resolve weight into $mg\sin\theta$ along the plane and $mg\cos\theta$ perpendicular to it. For a moving particle, friction has magnitude $\mu R$ and opposes motion. Momentum is $mv$; impulse is the change in momentum. In a direct collision, total signed momentum is conserved when external impulse is negligible.

misconceptions.statement: A moving particle needs a forward resultant force to keep moving.
misconceptions.refutation: With zero resultant force, velocity stays constant by Newton’s first law.
misconceptions.contrast: A resultant force changes velocity, not merely maintains it.

misconceptions.statement: Action and reaction cancel on one particle.
misconceptions.refutation: Newton’s third-law forces act on different bodies.
misconceptions.contrast: Only forces on the chosen particle belong in its $\sum F=ma$ equation.

misconceptions.statement: The same force equation applies unchanged after one connected particle hits the ground.
misconceptions.refutation: After contact, the string may become slack and the moving particle has a new force balance.
misconceptions.contrast: Split the motion into phases and carry the contact velocity into the next phase.

misconceptions.statement: Tension is an extra force on the combined two-particle system.
misconceptions.refutation: The two tension forces are internal and cancel when equations for the two particles are added.
misconceptions.contrast: Keep tension in each separate particle equation.

misconceptions.statement: Momentum is always positive, even when a particle reverses direction.
misconceptions.refutation: Momentum $mv$ has the signed direction of velocity in one dimension.
misconceptions.contrast: Choose a positive direction before writing collision equations.

misconceptions.statement: Kinetic energy must be conserved in every direct collision.
misconceptions.refutation: Momentum is conserved when external impulse is negligible; kinetic energy can change.
misconceptions.contrast: Use signed momentum before and after, without assuming restitution or energy conservation.

misconceptions.statement: The normal reaction on a slope always equals $mg$.
misconceptions.refutation: With no other perpendicular force or acceleration, $R=mg\cos\theta$.
misconceptions.contrast: Resolve forces perpendicular to the plane.

misconceptions.statement: Friction always acts down a rough plane.
misconceptions.refutation: Friction opposes the actual or impending relative motion.
misconceptions.contrast: A particle sliding down has friction up the plane; one sliding up has friction down it.

misconceptions.statement: Inextensible alone guarantees equal acceleration in every phase.
misconceptions.refutation: First check that the string is taut and the pulley fixed; a slack string no longer imposes that constraint.
misconceptions.contrast: Keep the original equations after impact. Instead, First check that the string is taut and the pulley fixed; a slack string no longer imposes that constraint.
misconceptions.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c3.2.pdf pp.7-8; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International%20Advanced%20Level/Mathematics/2018/Specification-and-Sample-Assessment/international-a-level-maths-spec.pdf (Issue 3, printed p.45, M1 section 4)

misconceptions.statement: Any individual force impulse equals momentum change.
misconceptions.refutation: Momentum change equals the sum of all force impulses; isolate one only after accounting for the others.
misconceptions.contrast: Remember the formula without its system boundary. Instead, Momentum change equals the sum of all force impulses; isolate one only after accounting for the others.
misconceptions.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c3.4.pdf pp.3-6; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International%20Advanced%20Level/Mathematics/2018/Specification-and-Sample-Assessment/international-a-level-maths-spec.pdf (Issue 3, printed p.45, M1 section 4)

misconceptions.refutation: Friction opposes relative sliding; an upward-moving slowing particle has friction and acceleration both downhill.
misconceptions.contrast: A sliding particle often happens to accelerate along its motion. Instead, Friction opposes relative sliding; an upward-moving slowing particle has friction and acceleration both downhill.

worked.problem: A 3 kg particle experiences a resultant force of 15 N along $\mathbf i$. Find its acceleration vector.

steps.do: Choose $\mathbf i$ as the positive direction.
steps.why: The signs of force and acceleration must use the same axis.
Newton’s second law uses the resultant force on this particle.
Divide each force component by the mass.

faded.problem: A 4 kg particle experiences a resultant force of 28 N along $\mathbf i$. Find its acceleration magnitude.

worked.problem: Masses 2 kg and 3 kg are connected by a light string over a smooth fixed pulley. Find the acceleration and tension.

steps.do: Take the 3 kg mass downward and the 2 kg mass upward as positive.
steps.why: Both particles have acceleration of the same magnitude.
The string tension acts opposite to each chosen positive direction.
Tension cancels because it is internal to the two-particle system.
Use one particle’s equation to recover the string tension.

faded.problem: Masses 1 kg and 4 kg hang over a smooth fixed pulley. Find their acceleration magnitude.

worked.problem: A 2 kg particle moves right at 5 m s^-1 and collides directly with a 3 kg particle moving left at 1 m s^-1. They stick together. Find their common velocity.

steps.do: Take right as positive, so the initial velocities are $+5$ and $-1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
steps.why: Momentum is a signed vector quantity along the line.
The collision is brief and external impulse is taken as negligible.

faded.problem: A 2 kg particle moving right at 6 m s^-1 sticks to a stationary 4 kg particle. Find their common speed.

worked.problem: A 2 kg particle slides down a rough $30^\circ$ plane with coefficient of friction $0.2$. Find its acceleration.

steps.do: Take down the plane as positive. Friction acts up the plane.
steps.why: Friction opposes the actual sliding direction.
There is no acceleration perpendicular to the plane.
The particle is moving, so the stated friction rule applies.
The weight component drives downhill motion and friction resists it.

faded.problem: A 3 kg particle slides down a rough 30 degree plane with coefficient of friction 0.1. Find its acceleration.

items.stem: A $[[m]]\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle has resultant force $[[F]]\,\mathrm{N}$ in the positive direction. Calculate its acceleration.
items.explanation: Newton’s second law gives $a=F/m$ in the direction of the resultant force.
hints: Identify the resultant, rather than one individual force.
Apply Newton’s second law to the particle.
Divide the resultant force by mass.

items.stem: A $[[m]]\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle has forces $[[P]]\mathbf i+[[Q]]\mathbf j$ newtons. Calculate the magnitude of its acceleration.
items.explanation: The acceleration vector is $(P\mathbf i+Q\mathbf j)/m$; its magnitude is $\sqrt{P^2+Q^2}/m$.
hints: Work component by component.
Find the magnitude of the resultant vector.
Use $\sum\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$.

items.stem: Explain Newton’s three laws and why an action–reaction pair does not cancel in a single particle’s equation.
items.explanation: Newton’s first law describes zero resultant, the second gives $\sum\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$, and the third concerns equal opposite forces on different bodies.
hints: Think about motion when the resultant is zero.
State the force–acceleration equation.
Name which body receives each interaction force.

rubric.point: With zero resultant force, a particle stays at rest or moves with constant velocity.
The resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
An interaction produces equal and opposite forces on different bodies.
Only forces on the selected particle enter its equation.

items.stem: Masses $[[m1]]$ kg and $[[m2]]$ kg hang on either side of a light string over a smooth fixed pulley, with $m2>m1$. Calculate their acceleration magnitude. Take $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
items.explanation: Adding the two separate equations eliminates tension: $(m_2-m_1)g=(m_1+m_2)a$.
hints: Draw one force diagram for each mass.
Give both particles the same acceleration magnitude.
Add the two $F=ma$ equations to eliminate tension.

items.stem: A $[[m]]$ kg particle slides down a smooth plane inclined at $[[theta]]$ degrees to the horizontal. Calculate its acceleration down the plane. Take $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
items.explanation: Resolving along the smooth plane gives $ma=mg\sin\theta$, so mass cancels.
hints: Resolve weight parallel to the slope.
There is no friction on a smooth plane.
Write $ma=mg\sin\theta$.

items.stem: Two particles initially move on a taut string over a smooth pulley. One hits the ground while the other is still moving. Explain how to find the subsequent motion.
items.explanation: The force system changes at impact. The velocity is continuous through the instant, but the later acceleration must come from a new force diagram.
hints: Split the motion at the impact instant.
Decide whether tension continues to act.
Use the impact velocity as the new initial velocity.

rubric.point: Use separate force equations while the string is taut and the same acceleration magnitude for both particles.
At impact carry the velocity forward, then check whether the string becomes slack.
For the later phase use the remaining particle’s new force balance and constant-acceleration equations.

items.stem: A $[[m]]$ kg particle changes velocity from $[[u]]$ to $[[v]]\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ along a chosen positive line. Calculate the signed impulse on it.
items.explanation: The impulse–momentum principle gives $J=mv-mu=m(v-u)$.
hints: Momentum has a direction sign.
Subtract initial momentum from final momentum.
Multiply the velocity change by mass.

items.stem: A $[[m1]]$ kg particle moves right at $[[u1]]\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and collides directly with a stationary $[[m2]]$ kg particle. They stick together. Calculate their common speed after collision.
items.explanation: Conservation of signed momentum gives $m_1u_1=(m_1+m_2)v$ for the joined particles.
hints: Choose right as positive.
Write total momentum before and after.
The joined mass is the sum of the two masses.

items.stem: Explain when momentum may be conserved in a direct collision and why kinetic energy need not be conserved.
items.explanation: Internal collision impulses cancel for the system. This supports momentum conservation without assuming an elastic collision or a restitution rule.
hints: Treat the two particles as one system.
Ask which impulses are external.
Keep velocity signs in the momentum equation.

rubric.point: Total momentum is conserved when the external impulse on the two-particle system is negligible.
Momentum is signed in a one-dimensional collision.
Kinetic energy can change to other forms during impact.

items.stem: A $[[m]]$ kg particle slides on a rough horizontal surface with coefficient of friction $[[mu]]$. Calculate the friction magnitude. Take $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
items.explanation: On the horizontal surface $R=mg$, so moving friction has magnitude $F=\mu R=\mu mg$.
hints: Find the normal reaction first.
Use $F=\mu R$ for a moving particle.
Friction opposes the sliding direction.

items.stem: A $[[m]]$ kg particle slides down a rough plane inclined at $[[theta]]$ degrees to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction is $[[mu]]$. Calculate its acceleration down the plane. Take $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
items.explanation: Here $R=mg\cos\theta$ and friction is up the plane. Thus $ma=mg\sin\theta-\mu mg\cos\theta$.
hints: Set axes parallel and perpendicular to the plane.
Find $R$ before calculating friction.
Because motion is down the plane, friction is up it.

items.stem: A particle is sliding up a rough incline. Explain the direction and magnitude of friction and how the normal reaction is found.
items.explanation: Friction opposes sliding, so it points downhill here. Resolve perpendicular to the slope to obtain $R$, then use $F=\mu R$.
hints: Use the actual direction of sliding.
Resolve perpendicular to the plane.
Use the coefficient only after finding the reaction.

rubric.point: Friction acts down the plane, opposite the upward motion.
Its magnitude is $F=\mu R$.
With only weight and reaction perpendicular to the plane, $R=mg\cos\theta$.

items.stem: Particles A and B of masses $3\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $5\,\mathrm{kg}$ hang on a light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley. Released from rest with the string taut, B falls $1.25\,\mathrm{m}$ before hitting the ground and remaining there. A stays clear of the pulley. Take $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Calculate (a) the acceleration before contact, (b) the speed at contact, and (c) the further distance A rises before first coming to rest. Explain the change of force model.
items.explanation: Adding the taut-string equations gives $a=2.45\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and $v=\sqrt{6.125}=2.47\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. A continues upward and the string slackens, so $T=0$ and its acceleration is $g$ downward; its further rise is $6.125/(2g)=0.3125\,\mathrm{m}$, or $0.313\,\mathrm{m}$.
hints: Draw separate force diagrams before contact.
Use the fall distance to find the contact speed.
After contact, decide whether the rising particle keeps the string taut.

scheme.point: A rises with the string slack, so $T=0$ and acceleration is $g$ downward.

items.stem: A $4\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle slides up a rough plane inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction is $0.20$; no force other than weight and contact forces acts. Take $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Calculate (a) the normal reaction and (b) the signed acceleration, taking up the plane as positive.
items.explanation: Perpendicular balance gives $R=4g\cos30^\circ=33.9\,\mathrm{N}$. Friction acts down the plane, so $4a=-4g\sin30^\circ-0.20R$ and $a=-6.60\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
hints: Resolve perpendicular to the plane first.
Friction opposes the upward sliding.
Both gravity along the plane and friction have negative components.

items.stem: A $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle moves right at $3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and collides directly with a $3\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle moving left at $4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. They stick together; external impulse is negligible. Taking right as positive, calculate (a) their common velocity and state its direction, and (b) the signed impulse on the $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle.
items.explanation: Signed momentum gives $2(3)+3(-4)=5v$, so $v=-1.20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, to the left. The impulse on the first particle is $2(-1.2-3)=-8.40\,\mathrm{N\,s}$.
hints: Give the initial leftward velocity a negative sign.
Use the combined mass after sticking.
For the impulse, use only the mass and velocity change of the specified particle.

items.stem: A $0.50\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle initially moves right at $5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and then moves left at $3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Taking right as positive, calculate the impulse on it.
items.explanation: $J=0.50(-3-5)=-4\,\mathrm{N\,s}$. Subtracting speeds instead of signed velocities gives the incorrect $-1\,\mathrm{N\,s}$; a positive impulse has the wrong direction.
hints: Choose the signed final velocity.
Impulse is final momentum minus initial momentum.
The final velocity is negative and the initial velocity is positive.

items.stem: The only forces on a $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle are $(8\mathbf i-3\mathbf j)\,\mathrm{N}$ and $(-2\mathbf i+11\mathbf j)\,\mathrm{N}$. Calculate (a) the resultant force and (b) the acceleration vector.
items.explanation: Adding components gives $\mathbf F=(6\mathbf i+8\mathbf j)\,\mathrm{N}$. Dividing each component by the mass gives $\mathbf a=(3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
hints: Add the force vectors component by component.
Apply Newton's second law to the resultant.
Divide both resultant components by the same mass.

scheme.point: Add the two forces component by component.

items.stem: A crate slides along a rough floor while a rope pulls it. State which pair of forces is a Newton's third-law pair.
items.explanation: The floor pushes the crate and the crate pushes the floor: these are opposite forces from the same interaction on different bodies. Every other option names two forces acting on the crate.
hints: Identify the body on which each force acts.
Third-law partners belong to one interaction.
Swap the acting body and the receiving body to identify the partner.

options.A: The weight of the crate and the normal force of the floor on the crate.
options.B: The normal force of the floor on the crate and the normal force of the crate on the floor.
options.C: The rope tension on the crate and friction on the crate.
options.D: The weight of the crate and the rope tension on the crate.

items.stem: A $5\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle slides right on a rough horizontal plane. A $20\,\mathrm{N}$ force acts rightward at angle $\alpha$ above the horizontal, where $\sin\alpha=3/5$ and $\cos\alpha=4/5$. The coefficient of friction is $0.25$. Take $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Calculate (a) the normal reaction, (b) the friction magnitude and (c) the acceleration to the right.
items.explanation: Vertical balance gives $R+20(3/5)=49$, so $R=37\,\mathrm{N}$. Friction is $0.25R=9.25\,\mathrm{N}$ leftward, hence $5a=20(4/5)-9.25$ and $a=1.35\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
hints: Resolve the applied force horizontally and vertically.
There is no vertical acceleration, but the applied force changes the reaction.
Find friction from the reaction before writing the horizontal equation.

items.stem: A particle slides up a rough incline, stops briefly, then slides back down. State the direction of friction while it is sliding in each phase; exclude the instant at rest.
items.explanation: Moving friction opposes the relative sliding: downhill during ascent and uphill during descent. Its direction is determined by velocity, so it reverses when the sliding direction reverses.
hints: Consider the two sliding phases separately.
Identify the velocity direction in each phase.
Place friction opposite the relative velocity along the plane.

options.A: Down the plane in both phases.
options.B: Up the plane in both phases.
options.C: Down the plane during ascent; up the plane during descent.
options.D: Up the plane during ascent; down the plane during descent.

flashcards.back: A body remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless acted on by a non-zero resultant force.

flashcards.front: State Newton’s second law for constant mass.
flashcards.back: The resultant force on a body equals its mass times acceleration, in the direction of the acceleration: $\sum\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$.
When two bodies interact, they exert forces on each other that are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
The impulse on a particle equals its change in momentum: $J=mv-mu$.

flashcards.front: When is momentum conserved for two colliding particles?
flashcards.back: Their total momentum is conserved when the resultant external impulse on the two-particle system is negligible.
The magnitude of friction is $F=\mu R$ for a particle moving relative to a rough surface; friction opposes motion.

M1-4.1.motivate: A particle can keep moving without a driving resultant force. Forces explain changes in motion, so start by identifying every force acting on the chosen body.
M1-4.1.establish: A force is an interaction measured in newtons. Newton's first law says a body stays at rest or continues at constant velocity if the resultant force is zero. For constant mass, Newton's second law is $\sum\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$: the acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force. In a plane, resolve the vector equation into $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j$ components. Newton's third law says two interacting bodies exert forces on each other that are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. These forces act on different bodies, so only one belongs in either body's force equation.
M1-4.1.connect: Constant acceleration links the force model to the kinematics equations. Once $a$ is found from the resultant force, use the appropriate equation of motion for the requested velocity, time or displacement.
M1-4.1.note:
- Zero resultant force means constant velocity, including rest.
- $\sum\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$ for constant mass.
- Third-law partners act on different bodies.
- In a plane, resolve force and acceleration by components.
M1-4.1.self_explain: Why can two equal and opposite third-law forces not cancel in the force equation for just one particle?
M1-4.1.plain_words: First choose one body. Add only the forces acting on it, then divide the resultant by its constant mass to find acceleration. Zero acceleration allows a nonzero constant velocity. Before this lesson, recall how to add signed vector components and how acceleration changes velocity.

terms.meaning: Vector sum of all forces acting on the chosen body.

terms.meaning: Rate of change of velocity; it follows resultant force, not necessarily velocity.

terms.meaning: Equal opposite interaction forces on two different bodies.
terms.spoken: force on B by A is opposite to force on A by B

forms.name: Explain zero resultant and third-law partners
wordings: Explain whether a moving particle needs a nonzero resultant force.
Identify the two bodies in a third-law force pair.
forms.example: Example: a puck moves at constant velocity on smooth horizontal ice. Stage 1: unchanged velocity gives $\mathbf a=0$. Stage 2: $\sum\mathbf F=m\mathbf a=0$ despite motion. Stage 3: weight and reaction both act on the puck, so are not third-law partners; the partner of the Earth pulling the puck is the puck pulling the Earth.
forms.check: A crate moves steadily on a level rough floor while a rope pulls it horizontally. Explain its horizontal resultant and identify the partner of the force exerted by the rope on the crate.
forms.answer: The horizontal resultant is zero because velocity is constant; the pull balances friction. The partner is the force exerted by the crate on the rope, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, acting on the rope rather than the crate.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c3.2.pdf pp.2-3,23-24; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International%20Advanced%20Level/Mathematics/2018/Specification-and-Sample-Assessment/international-a-level-maths-spec.pdf (Issue 3, printed p.45, M1 section 4)

rubric.point: Relate constant velocity to zero acceleration and hence zero horizontal resultant.
Identify the force exerted by the crate on the rope. Equal magnitude and opposite direction are valid supporting details, not required.

forms.name: Apply Newton’s second law by vector components
wordings: Find the acceleration of a particle subject to two constant vector forces.
forms.example: Example: the only forces on a $3\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle are $(7\mathbf i+2\mathbf j)\,\mathrm N$ and $(-1\mathbf i+7\mathbf j)\,\mathrm N$. Stage 1: add corresponding components to obtain $(6\mathbf i+9\mathbf j)\,\mathrm N$. Stage 2: $3\mathbf a=6\mathbf i+9\mathbf j$. Stage 3: $\mathbf a=(2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Its direction is that of the resultant, regardless of initial velocity.
forms.check: The only forces on a $4\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle are $(-8\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)\,\mathrm N$ and $(2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j)\,\mathrm N$. Find its acceleration as a vector.
forms.answer: $\sum\mathbf F=(-6\mathbf i+8\mathbf j)\,\mathrm N$, so $\mathbf a=(-1.5\mathbf i+2\mathbf j)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c3.2.pdf pp.2-3,23-24; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International%20Advanced%20Level/Mathematics/2018/Specification-and-Sample-Assessment/international-a-level-maths-spec.pdf (Issue 3, printed p.45, M1 section 4)

rubric.point: Add force components with their signs to obtain the resultant.
Apply the same mass to both components and state acceleration with units.
Give the vertical component as positive two metres per second squared.

misconceptions.idea: Zero resultant means the body must be at rest.
misconceptions.temptation: Confuse velocity with change in velocity.
misconceptions.fix: Zero resultant means constant velocity; rest is one possible constant velocity.

misconceptions.idea: Third-law partners cancel on a single body.
misconceptions.temptation: Both forces are equal and opposite.
misconceptions.fix: Label which body each force acts on before writing its equation.

M1-4.1.diagram_reason: The component equations and named interacting bodies are explicit in these forms; no additional registered vector or interaction-pair visual was reviewed for this pass.

M1-4.2.motivate: A string can make two particles move together, while a ground impact can suddenly change which forces act. Separate force diagrams and motion phases keep the model accurate.
M1-4.2.establish: For two particles joined by a light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley or peg, a taut string gives the same acceleration magnitude to both and the same tension along the string. Choose a positive direction for each body and apply $\sum F=ma$ separately. Add the equations to eliminate the internal tension, then substitute back to find it. On a plane inclined at $\theta$ to the horizontal, resolve weight into $mg\sin\theta$ down the plane and $mg\cos\theta$ perpendicular to it. A smooth plane has no friction; on a rough plane include friction opposing the motion. If one particle hits the ground, use its velocity at that instant as the starting velocity for a new phase. Check whether the string becomes slack, then redraw the remaining forces and solve the later motion.
M1-4.2.connect: The acceleration from Newton's second law feeds into constant-acceleration kinematics. At a force change, the velocity is carried across the phase boundary, while acceleration may change.
M1-4.2.note:
- Draw a separate force diagram for each particle.
- A taut light string gives one tension and equal acceleration magnitudes.
- Resolve slope weight as $mg\sin\theta$ parallel and $mg\cos\theta$ perpendicular.
- After impact, start a new force and kinematics phase.
M1-4.2.self_explain: Why can tension disappear when two connected-particle equations are added, yet still be needed to find the tension itself?
M1-4.2.plain_words: Use one force equation for each particle. A taut string constrains their motion; after contact, ask whether that constraint still holds. Before starting, recall simultaneous equations and the constant-acceleration equations. Use $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

terms.meaning: Negligible mass; together with a smooth pulley this permits one tension.
terms.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c3.2.pdf pp.7-8; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International%20Advanced%20Level/Mathematics/2018/Specification-and-Sample-Assessment/international-a-level-maths-spec.pdf (Issue 3, printed p.45, M1 section 4)

terms.meaning: Its total length does not change; when taut over a fixed pulley it gives equal endpoint speed and acceleration magnitudes.
terms.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c3.2.pdf pp.7-8; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International%20Advanced%20Level/Mathematics/2018/Specification-and-Sample-Assessment/international-a-level-maths-spec.pdf (Issue 3, printed p.45, M1 section 4)

terms.meaning: No friction at the pulley; the ideal light-string model uses equal tensions on the two sides.
terms.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c3.2.pdf pp.7-8; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International%20Advanced%20Level/Mathematics/2018/Specification-and-Sample-Assessment/international-a-level-maths-spec.pdf (Issue 3, printed p.45, M1 section 4)

terms.meaning: A taut string is stretched straight and can pull; a slack string cannot transmit tension.
terms.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c3.2.pdf pp.7-8; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International%20Advanced%20Level/Mathematics/2018/Specification-and-Sample-Assessment/international-a-level-maths-spec.pdf (Issue 3, printed p.45, M1 section 4)

forms.name: Separate connected-particle equations and string assumptions
wordings: Find the common acceleration and tension.
Explain the consequences of light, inextensible and smooth.
forms.example: Example: $4\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $6\,\mathrm{kg}$ particles hang on a taut light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley. Stage 1: take the heavier particle downward and lighter upward as positive. Stage 2: $6g-T=6a$ and $T-4g=4a$. Stage 3: addition gives $2g=10a$, hence $a=1.96\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Substitute back: $T=4(g+a)=47.0\,\mathrm N$ to three significant figures. The common acceleration requires tautness and inextensibility; equal tension uses the light string and smooth pulley.
forms.check: Particles of masses $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $5\,\mathrm{kg}$ hang on a taut light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley. Find acceleration and tension; state which assumptions justify equal acceleration magnitudes and a single tension.
forms.answer: $5g-T=5a$ and $T-2g=2a$ give $a=4.20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, with the heavier particle downward, and $T=28.0\,\mathrm N$. Tautness plus inextensibility gives equal acceleration magnitudes; the light string and smooth pulley give equal tensions.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c3.2.pdf pp.7-8; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International%20Advanced%20Level/Mathematics/2018/Specification-and-Sample-Assessment/international-a-level-maths-spec.pdf (Issue 3, printed p.45, M1 section 4)

rubric.point: Use a correct force method: either separate signed equations for both particles, or a whole-system acceleration equation followed by a particle equation for tension.
Solve for acceleration, heavier mass downward, and tension.
Obtain tension of twenty-eight newtons.
Distinguish the taut inextensible constraint from the light-string smooth-pulley tension assumptions.

forms.name: Change of phase after ground contact
wordings: Find the further rise after the heavier particle hits the ground.
Explain why the tension changes after contact.
forms.example: Example: $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $3\,\mathrm{kg}$ masses start from rest on a taut light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley. The heavier mass descends $0.80\,\mathrm m$ then stays on the ground; the lighter mass remains clear of the pulley. Stage 1: $a=(3-1)g/(3+1)=4.9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Stage 2: $v^2=2a(0.80)=7.84$. Stage 3: the lighter mass keeps moving upward at $2.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ immediately after contact, so the endpoint distance to the pulley shrinks and the string slackens. Its tension is zero and upward acceleration is $-g$. Stage 4: $0=7.84-2gh$ gives further rise $h=0.40\,\mathrm m$. Carry velocity across for the non-impacting mass, not the mass that strikes the ground.
forms.check: Masses $3\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $7\,\mathrm{kg}$ start from rest on a taut light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley. The heavier mass falls $1.50\,\mathrm m$ then stays on the ground. The lighter mass stays clear of the pulley. Find its speed at contact and its further rise, explaining the changed force model.
forms.answer: Before contact $a=3.92\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and $v^2=11.76$, so speed is $3.43\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The lighter particle continues upward while the grounded endpoint stays still, so the string slackens and $T=0$. The lighter particle has acceleration $-9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ upward-positive, giving $h=11.76/(2g)=0.600\,\mathrm m$. Its velocity is continuous at contact; its acceleration changes.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c3.2.pdf pp.7-8; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International%20Advanced%20Level/Mathematics/2018/Specification-and-Sample-Assessment/international-a-level-maths-spec.pdf (Issue 3, printed p.45, M1 section 4)

rubric.point: Obtain the first-phase acceleration using a correct force method, including a whole-system equation.
Use the fall distance to obtain the speed at contact.
Identify that the string is slack and tension is zero; credit the gravity-only model without requiring endpoint geometry.
Use gravity alone and the carried upward speed to obtain further rise.

forms.name: Resolve motion on a smooth incline
wordings: Find acceleration directly up or down a smooth plane.
forms.example: Example: a particle slides upward on a smooth plane at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal with no applied force. Stage 1: weight is vertical and reaction normal to the plane. Stage 2: no normal acceleration gives $R=mg\cos30^\circ$. Stage 3: upward-positive, $-mg\sin30^\circ=ma$, hence $a=-4.90\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; it slows while moving upward. Smooth means no friction.
forms.check: A $5\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle slides down a smooth plane with $\sin\theta=0.6$ and $\cos\theta=0.8$. Only weight and reaction act. Find reaction and acceleration down the plane.

rubric.point: Use the perpendicular component for reaction.
Resolve weight down the plane in Newton’s second law.
Give acceleration with direction and units.

misconceptions.idea: Inextensible alone guarantees equal acceleration in every phase.
misconceptions.temptation: Keep the original equations after impact.
misconceptions.fix: First check that the string is taut and the pulley fixed; a slack string no longer imposes that constraint.

misconceptions.idea: Both masses keep the same velocity across ground contact.
misconceptions.temptation: Apply continuity to the particle that collides with the ground.
misconceptions.fix: Only the non-impacting particle carries its velocity into the slack-string phase; the impacting one stops in this model.

M1-4.3.motivate: During a brief collision, large contact forces act for a short time. Momentum and impulse describe the motion change without needing the detailed force history.
M1-4.3.establish: A particle's momentum is $p=mv$, with velocity and momentum signed along the chosen one-dimensional axis. Impulse is force times time for a constant force, or more generally the change in momentum: $J=mv-mu$. This is the impulse–momentum principle. In a direct collision between two particles, their total momentum before equals their total momentum after when the resultant external impulse on the two-particle system is negligible. Write both particles' signed momenta before and after, then solve the resulting equation. If the particles stick, they share a final velocity. Do not assume kinetic energy conservation or use a restitution law; neither is required for these one-dimensional questions.
M1-4.3.connect: Newton's second law connects force with momentum change. The collision equation treats both particles as one system, so their internal impulses cancel.
M1-4.3.note:
- Momentum is signed: $p=mv$.
- Impulse equals change in momentum: $J=m(v-u)$.
- Negligible external impulse gives conservation of total momentum.
- Direct collisions here are one-dimensional; kinetic energy need not be conserved.
M1-4.3.self_explain: Why can total momentum be conserved when the two colliding particles exert large forces on each other?
M1-4.3.plain_words: Choose a positive direction before writing momentum. The sum of all external impulses changes a particle’s momentum. For two colliding particles, internal impulses cancel, so total momentum is conserved when external impulse is negligible. Recall signed velocity before starting.

terms.meaning: Mass times signed velocity in one dimension.
terms.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c3.4.pdf pp.3-6; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International%20Advanced%20Level/Mathematics/2018/Specification-and-Sample-Assessment/international-a-level-maths-spec.pdf (Issue 3, printed p.45, M1 section 4)

terms.meaning: Sum of impulses of all forces on the chosen body; this equals change of momentum.

terms.spoken: total signed momentum before equals total signed momentum after when external impulse is negligible

forms.name: Signed impulse and reversal
wordings: Find the impulse and constant resultant force when a particle reverses direction.
Distinguish the impulse of one force from the total impulse.
forms.example: Example: a $0.40\,\mathrm{kg}$ ball initially moves right at $5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and leaves left at $3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ after $0.10\,\mathrm s$. Stage 1: right-positive gives $u=5$, $v=-3$. Stage 2: $J_{net}=0.40(-3-5)=-3.2\,\mathrm{N\,s}$. Stage 3: if resultant force is constant, it is $-32\,\mathrm N$, leftward. The net impulse $-3.2\,\mathrm{N\,s}$ equals the contact-force impulse only when other impulses are negligible; otherwise subtract their signed sum from the net impulse to find it.
forms.check: A $0.60\,\mathrm{kg}$ ball initially travels left at $4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and after $0.20\,\mathrm s$ travels right at $1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Find net impulse and constant resultant force. Explain whether this determines the impulse of a particular contact force when another force has non-negligible impulse.
forms.answer: Right-positive: $u=-4$, $v=1$. Net impulse is $0.60(1-(-4))=3.0\,\mathrm{N\,s}$ rightward. Constant resultant force is $3.0/0.20=15\,\mathrm N$ rightward. A contact impulse alone is not determined unless the other impulse is known; subtract the other impulse from the net impulse.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c3.4.pdf pp.3-6; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International%20Advanced%20Level/Mathematics/2018/Specification-and-Sample-Assessment/international-a-level-maths-spec.pdf (Issue 3, printed p.45, M1 section 4)

rubric.point: Use opposite signs for initial and final velocities.
Calculate the signed momentum change with its direction.
Divide net impulse by duration for resultant force.
Distinguish net impulse from the contact impulse by accounting for other forces.

forms.name: Signed direct collision with negligible external impulse
wordings: Find a common velocity when particles coalesce.
Find an unknown velocity after a direct collision.
forms.example: Example: on a smooth horizontal line, a $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle moving right at $3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ meets a $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle moving left at $4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; they stick. External impulse along the line is negligible. Stage 1: right-positive gives $u_1=3$, $u_2=-4$. Stage 2: $2(3)+1(-4)=(2+1)v$. Stage 3: $v=2/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, rightward. The particles share velocity because they stick; kinetic energy conservation is not assumed.
forms.check: A $1.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle moves right at $2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and a $2.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle moves left at $4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ on the same smooth horizontal line. They collide and stick, with negligible external impulse along the line. Find and interpret their common velocity. State whether kinetic energy must be conserved.
forms.answer: Right-positive: $1.5(2)+2.5(-4)=4v$, so $v=-1.75\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, or $1.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ leftward to two significant figures. The negative sign means leftward motion. Sticking does not conserve kinetic energy; total signed momentum is conserved because external impulse is negligible.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c3.4.pdf pp.3-6; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International%20Advanced%20Level/Mathematics/2018/Specification-and-Sample-Assessment/international-a-level-maths-spec.pdf (Issue 3, printed p.45, M1 section 4)

rubric.point: Use negligible external impulse to conserve total signed momentum.
Use a common final velocity for the combined mass.
Obtain $1.75\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ leftward (or $1.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to two significant figures), with any sign consistent with the chosen positive axis.
Do not assume kinetic energy conservation for a sticking collision.

misconceptions.idea: Subtract speeds to find momentum change during reversal.
misconceptions.temptation: Both speeds were given positive in the question.
misconceptions.fix: Assign signed velocities first; the momentum change includes reversal.

misconceptions.idea: Any individual force impulse equals momentum change.
misconceptions.temptation: Remember the formula without its system boundary.
misconceptions.fix: Momentum change equals the sum of all force impulses; isolate one only after accounting for the others.

misconceptions.idea: Momentum conservation also guarantees kinetic energy conservation.
misconceptions.temptation: Use the same conservation word for both.
misconceptions.fix: External impulse controls momentum; collisions can transfer kinetic energy into other forms.

M1-4.4.motivate: A surface pushes perpendicular to itself and resists sliding along itself. On a slope, finding the perpendicular push is essential before calculating friction.
M1-4.4.establish: The normal reaction $R$ acts perpendicular to the contact surface. The coefficient of friction $\mu$ relates the magnitude of friction to this reaction for a moving particle: $F=\mu R$. Friction acts opposite to the actual relative motion. On a horizontal surface without other vertical forces, $R=mg$. On a plane inclined at $\theta$ with no other perpendicular force or acceleration, $R=mg\cos\theta$. Resolve forces along the plane after finding $R$. A particle sliding down has friction up the slope; a particle sliding up has friction down the slope. The formula describes friction during motion here, so do not replace it with a guess about direction or with $R=mg$ on an incline.
M1-4.4.connect: Use the resolved friction force in Newton's second-law equation along the surface. The resulting acceleration can then be used in the constant-acceleration equations.
M1-4.4.note:
- For a moving particle, friction magnitude is $F=\mu R$.
- Friction opposes relative motion.
- Resolve perpendicular to find $R$; on a simple slope, $R=mg\cos\theta$.
- Then apply $\sum F=ma$ along the surface.
M1-4.4.self_explain: Why does friction point down the plane when a particle is sliding upward?
M1-4.4.plain_words: Find the force perpendicular to the surface first; then calculate sliding friction from it. Friction opposes sliding, which can differ from the direction of acceleration. Recall resolving weight parallel and perpendicular to a slope before starting.

terms.meaning: Contact force perpendicular to the surface.

forms.name: Moving friction on an incline
wordings: Find the reaction, friction and acceleration of a sliding particle.
Explain the friction direction for motion up or down a rough plane.
forms.example: Example: a $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle slides upward on a $30^\circ$ rough plane with $\mu=0.20$; only weight, reaction and friction act. Stage 1: the registered diagram shows friction down the slope because sliding is upward. Stage 2: perpendicular balance gives $R=2g\cos30^\circ=16.97\,\mathrm N$. Stage 3: $F=0.20R=3.39\,\mathrm N$. Stage 4: upward-positive, $-2g\sin30^\circ-F=2a$, giving $a=-6.60\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. If the particle later slides down, friction reverses to point uphill; at rest use a separate static model, not an automatic sliding equation.
forms.check: A $4\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle slides down a rough plane with $\sin\theta=0.6$, $\cos\theta=0.8$ and $\mu=0.25$. Only weight, reaction and friction act. Find reaction, friction magnitude and acceleration. An additional force is then applied parallel to the plane while the particle continues sliding down. Find the force needed to make its velocity constant.
forms.answer: $R=4g(0.8)=31.36\,\mathrm N$ and $F=0.25R=7.84\,\mathrm N$, uphill. Down-slope positive: $4g(0.6)-7.84=4a$, so $a=3.92\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ downhill. For constant velocity the resultant is zero, so the additional force is $4g(0.6)-7.84=15.68\,\mathrm N$ uphill, or $15.7\,\mathrm N$ to three significant figures.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/XMA01 mechanics-1/XMA01 c3.3.pdf pp.8-9; https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International%20Advanced%20Level/Mathematics/2018/Specification-and-Sample-Assessment/international-a-level-maths-spec.pdf (Issue 3, printed p.45, M1 section 4)

rubric.point: Resolve perpendicular with zero normal acceleration to find reaction.
Calculate friction from reaction and oppose downward sliding.
Use the signed parallel resultant to find acceleration.
Set the resultant along the plane to zero and find an additional force of $15.68\,\mathrm N$ uphill, accepting suitable rounding.

misconceptions.idea: Reaction is always equal to weight.
misconceptions.temptation: Reuse the horizontal formula on a slope.
misconceptions.fix: Resolve perpendicular; other applied forces may also change reaction.

misconceptions.temptation: A sliding particle often happens to accelerate along its motion.
misconceptions.fix: Friction opposes relative sliding; an upward-moving slowing particle has friction and acceleration both downhill.
